cards.front: What is an import?
back: A good or service bought from another country.

cards.front: What does a population pyramid show?
back: The age and sex structure of a population.

cards.front: Define immigration.
back: Movement into a country to live.

cards.front: What is suburbanisation?
back: Movement of people or activities from the inner city to the urban edge.

cards.front: Name one indicator of development within the UK.
back: Income.

cards.front: Which city is the major UK city case study in this course?
back: Leeds.

cards.front: Explain why using income alone may give a misleading picture of development.
back: Income does not show health, education or access to services.
An average can hide large differences between people or neighbourhoods.

cards.front: Give two reasons why an area with good infrastructure may attract businesses.
back: Transport links make workers, customers and goods easier to reach.
Reliable broadband helps firms communicate and provide digital services.

cards.front: Explain why the UK population is ageing.
back: People live longer because death rates have fallen.
Lower birth rates mean young people form a smaller share of the population.

cards.front: Give one social and one economic benefit of immigration.
back: Social: migrants can add cultural diversity.
Economic: migrants can fill skills gaps, work and pay taxes.

cards.front: Explain one possible consequence of counter-urbanisation for a rural settlement.
back: Housing demand may rise as people move in.
This can increase prices and make homes less affordable for existing residents.

cards.front: Give two challenges created by rapid city growth.
back: Increased demand for affordable housing.
More congestion and pressure on transport.

cards.front: Explain one reason why development varies across the UK.
back: Areas with poor transport or digital connections are less accessible.
Firms may invest elsewhere because costs or travel times are lower.
This reduces job opportunities and income in the less connected area.

cards.front: Explain one challenge caused by an ageing population.
back: A larger older population increases demand for healthcare and social care.
These services require more workers and public spending.
With fewer workers per dependent person, funding them can become harder.

cards.front: Explain how migration can change the character of a city.
back: Migrants bring languages, food, beliefs and traditions.
They may establish businesses and community services.
These changes make neighbourhoods and the city's workforce more diverse.

cards.front: Explain how the decline of the docks affected Salford Quays.
back: Larger container ships and competition from coastal ports reduced dock activity.
The docks closed in 1982, removing dock and linked industrial jobs.
Unemployment, polluted water and derelict land damaged the area's environment and image.

cards.front: Explain how government policy and infrastructure can reduce uneven development.
back: Government can fund regeneration, education or business support in weaker areas.
These policies can create jobs and improve skills.
Better roads, rail and broadband connect people and firms to markets.
Improved accessibility can attract investment and raise incomes.

cards.front: Explain two possible impacts of re-urbanisation.
back: Reusing brownfield land can bring homes, jobs and improved public spaces back to an inner city.
Rising demand may increase rents and house prices, so some lower-income residents may be displaced or excluded.

cards.front: Explain how regeneration changed Salford Quays.
back: Public investment reclaimed land, cleaned the waterfront and improved transport and public space.
The Lowry opened in 2000 and MediaCity in 2011, attracting visitors, broadcasters and creative firms.
MediaCity now contains major broadcasters and more than 250 creative and technology businesses.
However, expensive housing and skilled jobs mean benefits are not shared equally with nearby communities.

cards.front: Explain why Leeds is important at more than one scale.
back: Leeds had about 812,000 residents in 2021 and around 471,000 people work there, making it a major regional employment and service centre.
Finance, retail, healthcare, universities and culture attract people from across northern England.
Rail and motorway links connect firms and workers to other UK cities.
Universities and internationally connected businesses also attract overseas students, skills and investment.
